claim: RIPK1, RIPK3, and MLKL cause a form of programmed necrotic cell death in mammals termed necroptosis.
source: A pair of kinases, RIPK1 and RIPK3, as well as the RIPK3 substrate MLKL cause a form of programmed necrotic cell death in mammals termed necroptosis.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by citations throughout the manuscript (Christofferson and Yuan, 2010; Vandenabeele et al., 2010).

claim: Male reproductive organs of Ripk3-knockout mice retain youthful morphology and function into advanced age.
source: We report here that male reproductive organs of both Ripk3- and Mlkl-knockout mice retain 'youthful' morphology and function into advanced age, while those of age-matched wild-type mice deteriorate.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple experimental observations including histology, weight measurements, and fertility tests shown in Figures 1 and 4.

claim: Male reproductive organs of Mlkl-knockout mice retain youthful morphology and function into advanced age.
source: We report here that male reproductive organs of both Ripk3- and Mlkl-knockout mice retain 'youthful' morphology and function into advanced age, while those of age-matched wild-type mice deteriorate.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 4 showing seminal vesicle weights, testosterone levels, and fertility rates.

claim: RIPK3 phosphorylation of MLKL is detected in spermatogonial stem cells in the testes of old but not young wild-type mice.
source: The RIPK3 phosphorylation of MLKL, the activation marker of necroptosis, is detected in spermatogonial stem cells in the testes of old but not in young wild-type mice.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 2C, D, and F showing p-MLKL staining in 18-month-old but not 4-month-old wild-type testes.

claim: Local necroptotic stimulus to testes of young wild-type mice causes accelerated aging of reproductive organs.
source: When the testes of young wild-type mice are given a local necroptotic stimulus, their reproductive organs showed accelerated aging.
evidence: This is supported by TSZ injection experiments shown in Figures 5 and 6, demonstrating seminal vesicle enlargement and seminiferous tubule depletion.

claim: Feeding wild-type mice with an RIPK1 inhibitor prior to the normal onset of age-related changes blocks the appearance of signs of aging in reproductive organs.
source: Feeding of wild-type mice with an RIPK1 inhibitor prior to the normal onset of age-related changes in their reproductive organs blocked the appearance of signs of aging.
evidence: This is demonstrated by RIPA-56 feeding experiments in Figure 7, showing maintained fertility, testosterone levels, and seminiferous tubule integrity.

claim: Necroptosis in testes promotes the aging-associated deterioration of the male reproductive system in mice.
source: Thus, necroptosis in testes promotes the aging-associated deterioration of the male reproductive system in mice.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the combined evidence of knockout mice phenotypes, TSZ injection experiments, and RIPK1 inhibitor studies.

claim: 18-month-old Ripk3-knockout mice weigh significantly less than age-matched wild-type mice.
source: The average weight of 18-month-old wild-type mice was 46 grams, significantly more than of 37 grams of weight of the age-matched Ripk3-knockout mice (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is directly measured and shown in Figure 1B with statistical significance.

claim: The weights of 4-month-old wild-type and Ripk3-knockout mice are indistinguishable.
source: The weights of 4-month-old wild-type and Ripk3-knockout mice, on the other hand, were indistinguishable (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B with no significant difference between groups.

claim: Seminal vesicles from 18-month-old wild-type mice weigh between ~1,000 mg to 4,500 mg.
source: The weights of the seminal vesicles from 18-month-old wild-type mice (n = 33) ranged from ~1,000 mg to 4,500 mg, while the weights of the same organ from the age-matched Ripk3-knockout mice (n = 30) were mostly below 1,000 mg (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is directly measured and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Seminal vesicles from 18-month-old Ripk3-knockout mice weigh mostly below 1,000 mg.
source: The weights of the seminal vesicles from 18-month-old wild-type mice (n = 33) ranged from ~1,000 mg to 4,500 mg, while the weights of the same organ from the age-matched Ripk3-knockout mice (n = 30) were mostly below 1,000 mg (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is directly measured and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Seminal vesicles become enlarged as mice get old due to secondary growth in response to declining testis functions.
source: It is known that seminal vesicles become enlarged as mice get old, presumably due to secondary growth in response to declining of testis functions that is similar to prostate hypertrophy in human (Finch and Girgis, 1974; Pettan-Brewer and Treuting, 2011).
evidence: This is stated as known information and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The difference in seminal vesicles between wild-type and Ripk3-knockout mice becomes noticeable after one year of life.
source: The difference in seminal vesicles from wild-type and Ripk3-knockout mice become noticeable after one year of life, and become increasingly evident over time.
evidence: This is supported by the time-course data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Seminal vesicles from wild-type mice continue to grow from 4 months to 24 months.
source: The seminal vesicles from wild-type mice continue to grow, whereas the seminal vesicles from the Ripk3-knockout mice did not change in size from 4 months to 24 months (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B with measurements at multiple time points.

claim: Seminal vesicles from Ripk3-knockout mice did not change in size from 4 months to 24 months.
source: The seminal vesicles from wild-type mice continue to grow, whereas the seminal vesicles from the Ripk3-knockout mice did not change in size from 4 months to 24 months (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B with measurements at multiple time points.

claim: The epithelium of seminal vesicles from 18-month-old wild-type mice shows irregularities with spaces separating the epithelium and the liquid compartment.
source: Close examination revealed that the epithelium of the seminal vesicles from 18-month-old wild-type mice showed irregularities, with spaces separating the epithelium and the liquid compartment, whereas the seminal-vesicle epithelial cells from the age-matched Ripk3-knockout mice were tightly packed, just as they are in young mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This is observed in histological sections shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Seminal-vesicle epithelial cells from 18-month-old Ripk3-knockout mice are tightly packed, just as they are in young mice.
source: Close examination revealed that the epithelium of the seminal vesicles from 18-month-old wild-type mice showed irregularities, with spaces separating the epithelium and the liquid compartment, whereas the seminal-vesicle epithelial cells from the age-matched Ripk3-knockout mice were tightly packed, just as they are in young mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This is observed in histological sections shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: By 18 months of age, wild-type testes start to appear atrophic and weigh less than Ripk3-knockout testes.
source: By the time mice reached 18 months of age, the wild-type testes started to appear atrophic, and weighed less than Ripk3-knockout testes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and E with weight measurements and images.

claim: Testosterone level shows a dramatic drop as wild-type mice age from 4 to 18 months.
source: Consistently, the testosterone level showed a dramatic drop as wild-type mice aged from 4 to 18 months, whereas the testosterone levels hardly decreased at all in Ripk3-knockout mice over the same period (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is measured by ELISA and shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Testosterone levels hardly decrease in Ripk3-knockout mice as they age from 4 to 18 months.
source: Consistently, the testosterone level showed a dramatic drop as wild-type mice aged from 4 to 18 months, whereas the testosterone levels hardly decreased at all in Ripk3-knockout mice over the same period (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is measured by ELISA and shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The typical age-related increase in sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) that occurs in wild-type mice is not observed in Ripk3-knockout mice.
source: Moreover, the typical age-related increase in sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) (Vermeulen et al., 1996) that is known to occur in wild-type mice was not observed in Ripk3-knockout mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is measured by ELISA and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, with citation to previous literature.

claim: The levels of LH and FSH do not differ between wild-type and Ripk3-knockout mice and both drop significantly as mice age from 4 months to 18 months.
source: Interestingly, the levels of two endocrine factors secreted by the pituitary gland, LH and FSH (Cooke and Saunders, 2002), did not differ between wild-type and Ripk3-knockout mice; both dropped significantly as mice aged from 4 months to 18 months (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: This is measured by ELISA and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and C.

claim: The difference in aging of reproductive system between old wild-type and Ripk3-knockout mice may result from local changes in testis.
source: This finding indicated that the difference in aging of reproductive system between old wild-type and Ripk3-knockout mice may result from local changes in testis.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that pituitary hormones (LH and FSH) are similar between genotypes while local testis changes differ.

claim: Many seminiferous tubules from 18-month-old wild-type mice have lost cells, giving them an 'empty' appearance.
source: When testes from 4-month-old and 18-month-old wild-type and Ripk3-knockout mice were dissected and their cross sections were examined under a microscope, cells in many of the seminiferous tubules from the 18-month-old wild-type mice were lost, given the seminiferous tubules an 'empty' appearance (Figure 1F and G).
evidence: This is observed in histological sections shown in Figure 1F and quantified in Figure 1G.

claim: The central lumens of seminiferous tubules of 4-month-old wild-type and Ripk3-knockout mice are fully surrounded with cells and filled with sperm.
source: In contrast, the central lumens of the seminiferous tubules of 4-month-old wild-type and Ripk3-knockout mice are fully surrounded with cells, and are filled with sperm.
evidence: This is observed in histological sections shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The seminiferous tubules of 18-month-old Ripk3-knockout mice look no different than those of 4-month-old mice.
source: Strikingly, the seminiferous tubules of 18-month-old Ripk3-knockout mice looked no different than those of 4-month-old mice (Figure 1F and G).
evidence: This is observed in histological sections shown in Figure 1F and quantified in Figure 1G.

claim: Close to half of seminiferous tubules of 36-month-old wild-type mice are empty.
source: Even more dramatically, when testis sections from 36-month-old mice were examined, close to half of seminiferous tubules of wild-type mice were empty, while more than 90% of those from the Ripk3-knockout mice still appeared normal (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is observed and quantified in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: More than 90% of seminiferous tubules from 36-month-old Ripk3-knockout mice still appear normal.
source: Even more dramatically, when testis sections from 36-month-old mice were examined, close to half of seminiferous tubules of wild-type mice were empty, while more than 90% of those from the Ripk3-knockout mice still appeared normal (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is observed and quantified in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Most epididymides from 18-month-old wild-type mice have few sperm.
source: Similar to the phenotypes observed in the seminiferous tubules, most of the epididymides from 18-month-old wild-type mice had few sperm, whereas most of the epididymides of age-matched Ripk3-knockout mice were full of sperm (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This is observed in histological sections shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5A.

claim: Most epididymides of 18-month-old Ripk3-knockout mice are full of sperm.
source: Similar to the phenotypes observed in the seminiferous tubules, most of the epididymides from 18-month-old wild-type mice had few sperm, whereas most of the epididymides of age-matched Ripk3-knockout mice were full of sperm (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This is observed in histological sections shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5A.

claim: Sperm counts in epididymes increase steadily during development and peak at four months of age.
source: The sperm counts in epididymes increased steadily during development and peaked at four months of age, and there was little difference in the sperm counts between wild-type and Ripk3-knockout mice up to this time (Figure 1—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: This is measured and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5B.

claim: There is little difference in sperm counts between wild-type and Ripk3-knockout mice up to four months of age.
source: The sperm counts in epididymes increased steadily during development and peaked at four months of age, and there was little difference in the sperm counts between wild-type and Ripk3-knockout mice up to this time (Figure 1—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: This is measured and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5B.

claim: Sperm counts of wild-type mice start to decline after four months of age.
source: The sperm counts of wild-type mice then started to decline, while those of Ripk3-knockout mice remained steady until 12 months of age.
evidence: This is measured and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5B.

claim: Sperm counts of Ripk3-knockout mice remain steady until 12 months of age.
source: The sperm counts of wild-type mice then started to decline, while those of Ripk3-knockout mice remained steady until 12 months of age.
evidence: This is measured and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5B.

claim: At 24 months, the sperm counts of Ripk3-knockout mice are still comparable with those of 4-month-old wild-type mice.
source: Even at 24 months, the sperm counts of Ripk3-knockout mice were still comparable with those of 4-month-old wild-type mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: This is measured and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5B.

claim: Both wild-type and Ripk3-knockout 4-month-old male mice are fully fertile.
source: As summarized in Figure 1H, both wild-type and Ripk3-knockout 4-month-old male mice were fully fertile, and both groups sired a similar number of pups (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is shown in the fertility test results in Figure 1H.

claim: For 13-month-old mice, only 9 of 20 (45%) wild-type males sired pups.
source: However, for 13-month-old mice, only 9 of the 20 (45%)wild-type male mice sired pups, while 18 out of 23 (78%)Ripk3-knockout males remained fertile (Figure 1H and Figure 1—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: This is shown in the fertility test results in Figure 1H.

claim: For 13-month-old mice, 18 out of 23 (78%) Ripk3-knockout males remained fertile.
source: However, for 13-month-old mice, only 9 of the 20 (45%)wild-type male mice sired pups, while 18 out of 23 (78%)Ripk3-knockout males remained fertile (Figure 1H and Figure 1—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: This is shown in the fertility test results in Figure 1H.

claim: Only 4 out of 22 (18%) wild-type male mice were still fertile at 18 months of age.
source: The difference was even more obvious with the 18-month-old male mice. Only 4 out of 22 (18%)wild-type male mice were still fertile at this age, whereas 15 out of 22 (68%)Ripk3-knockout male mice remained fertile (Figure 1H and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is shown in the fertility test results in Figure 1H.

claim: 15 out of 22 (68%) Ripk3-knockout male mice remained fertile at 18 months of age.
source: The difference was even more obvious with the 18-month-old male mice. Only 4 out of 22 (18%)wild-type male mice were still fertile at this age, whereas 15 out of 22 (68%)Ripk3-knockout male mice remained fertile (Figure 1H and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is shown in the fertility test results in Figure 1H.

claim: Wild-type mice on average lose the ability to sire offspring around 16 months.
source: Monitoring of the age at which each male sired its last litter showed that wild-type mice on average lost the ability to sire offspring around 16 months, while the Ripk3-knockout mice did not lose this ability until 22 months (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is measured in the reproductive longevity experiment shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Ripk3-knockout mice do not lose the ability to sire offspring until 22 months.
source: Monitoring of the age at which each male sired its last litter showed that wild-type mice on average lost the ability to sire offspring around 16 months, while the Ripk3-knockout mice did not lose this ability until 22 months (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is measured in the reproductive longevity experiment shown in Figure 1I.

claim: No differences were observed between wild-type and age-matched Ripk3-knockout mice in major organs during the aging process.
source: To see if delay of aging phenotype was restricted to the reproductive system, we conducted histological analysis of major organs including small intestines, spleen, lung, liver, large intestines, kidney, heart, and brain of wild-type and Ripk3-knockout mice aged 8 weeks, 4 months, 18 months, and 24 months. We observed no differences between wild-type and age-matched Ripk3-knockout mice during the aging process (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is observed in histological sections shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: Progenies sired by aged Ripk3-knockout mice are less healthy than progenies sired by young males, with higher rates of prenatal and postnatal death.
source: However, when we examined the progenies sired by the aged Ripk3-knockout mice at a time wild-type mice had lost most of their reproductive activity, we found that they were less healthy no matter they were sired by wild-type or Ripk3-knockout mice than the progenies sired by young males, with higher rates of prenatal and postnatal death (Figure 1—figure supplement 7A and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is measured and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7A.

claim: The level of 8-hydroxydeoxyguanosine (8-OHdG) is significantly higher in the sperm of 18-month-old wild type and Ripk3-knockout mice than in 4-month-old mice.
source: A study into the possible reason for the unhealthy offspring revealed accumulated oxidative damage in the sperm DNA of aged Ripk3-knockout mice, measured as the level of 8-hydroxydeoxyguanosine (8-OHdG), a biomarker for the oxidative damage of DNA (Chigurupati et al., 2008; Johnson et al., 2015; Paul et al., 2011), was significantly higher in the sperm of 18-month-old wild type and Ripk3-knockout mice than in 4-month-old mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 7B and C).
evidence: This is measured by immunohistochemistry and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7B and C.

claim: The difference in whole body weight of 18-month-old wild-type and Ripk3-knockout mice is mainly due to the difference in their seminal vesicles and fat tissues.
source: The difference in whole body weight of 18-month-old wild-type and Ripk3-knockout mice was mainly due to the difference in their seminal vesicles and fat tissues (Figure 1—figure supplement 8A–D).
evidence: This is measured and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 8A–D.

claim: Cells inside wild-type seminiferous tubules stain positively with anti-RIPK3 antibody.
source: We noted that the cells inside wild-type seminiferous tubules were stained positively with anti-RIPK3 antibody (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is observed in immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: No RIPK3 staining is seen in the seminiferous tubules of Ripk3-knockout mice.
source: In contrast, no staining was seen in the seminiferous tubules of Ripk3-knockout mice, confirming the specificity of the antibody (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is observed in immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and confirms antibody specificity.

claim: RIPK3 is expressed in germ line spermatogonia expressing UTF1.
source: RIPK3 expression was apparent in germ line spermatogonia expressing UTF1 (Jung et al., 2014; van Bragt et al., 2008) and in Sertoli cells expressing GATA-1 (Tsai et al., 2006).
evidence: This is shown by co-immunostaining in Figure 2A with cell-type specific markers.

claim: RIPK3 is expressed in Sertoli cells expressing GATA-1.
source: RIPK3 expression was apparent in germ line spermatogonia expressing UTF1 (Jung et al., 2014; van Bragt et al., 2008) and in Sertoli cells expressing GATA-1 (Tsai et al., 2006).
evidence: This is shown by co-immunostaining in Figure 2A with cell-type specific markers.

claim: Testosterone-producing Leydig cells marked by HSD3B1 do not express RIPK3.
source: The testosterone-producing Leydig cells (marked by the HSD3B1(Chang et al., 2011) located outside of seminiferous tubules, however, did not express RIPK3 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown by co-immunostaining in Figure 2A with cell-type specific markers.

claim: Primary spermatocytes marked by SMAD3 express RIPK3.
source: Moreover, the primary spermatocytes within seminiferous tubules that were not marked by IHC were now clearly visible when stained with the specific marker SMAD3 (Hentrich et al., 2011), and these cells expressed RIPK3 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown by co-immunostaining in Figure 2B with cell-type specific markers.

claim: Phosphorylated MLKL (phospho-MLKL) is detected in seminiferous tubules in cells surrounding the center lumens in testes of 18-month-old wild-type mice.
source: Phosphorylated MLKL (phospho-MLKL) was detected in seminiferous tubules in cells surrounding the center lumens in testes of 18-month-old wild-type mice, whereas no phospho-MLKL was detected in the same tissue area of 4-month-old wild-type mice, nor in 18-month-old Ripk3-knockout or Mlkl-knockout mice (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown by immunohistochemistry in Figure 2C and quantified in Figure 2D.

claim: No phospho-MLKL is detected in testes of 4-month-old wild-type mice.
source: Phosphorylated MLKL (phospho-MLKL) was detected in seminiferous tubules in cells surrounding the center lumens in testes of 18-month-old wild-type mice, whereas no phospho-MLKL was detected in the same tissue area of 4-month-old wild-type mice, nor in 18-month-old Ripk3-knockout or Mlkl-knockout mice (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown by immunohistochemistry in Figure 2C and quantified in Figure 2D.

claim: No phospho-MLKL is detected in testes of 18-month-old Ripk3-knockout mice.
source: Phosphorylated MLKL (phospho-MLKL) was detected in seminiferous tubules in cells surrounding the center lumens in testes of 18-month-old wild-type mice, whereas no phospho-MLKL was detected in the same tissue area of 4-month-old wild-type mice, nor in 18-month-old Ripk3-knockout or Mlkl-knockout mice (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown by immunohistochemistry in Figure 2C and quantified in Figure 2D.

claim: No phospho-MLKL is detected in testes of 18-month-old Mlkl-knockout mice.
source: Phosphorylated MLKL (phospho-MLKL) was detected in seminiferous tubules in cells surrounding the center lumens in testes of 18-month-old wild-type mice, whereas no phospho-MLKL was detected in the same tissue area of 4-month-old wild-type mice, nor in 18-month-old Ripk3-knockout or Mlkl-knockout mice (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown by immunohistochemistry in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Phospho-MLKL is detected by western blotting in extracts from testes of 18- and 24-month-old wild-type mice but not in extracts from age-matched Ripk3-knockout mice.
source: Consistently, phospho-MLKL was detected by western blotting in extracts from testes of 18- and 24-month-old wild-type mice but not in extracts from age-matched Ripk3-knockout mice (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is shown by western blot in Figure 2E.

claim: Spermatogonia expressing UTF1 are co-stained with anti-phospho-MLKL antibody in aged testes.
source: As shown in Figure 2F, spermatogonia that specifically expressing UTF1 were co-stained with the anti-phospho-MLKL antibody.
evidence: This is shown by co-immunostaining in Figure 2F.

claim: Sertoli cells do not show phospho-MLKL staining in aged testes even though they express RIPK3.
source: On the other hand, Sertoli cells did not show phospho-MLKL staining even though they do express RIPK3.
evidence: This is shown by co-immunostaining in Figure 2F.

claim: Leydig cells do not stain with the phosphor-MLKL antibody in aged testes.
source: Not surprisingly, Leydig cells that do not have RIPK3 expression also did not stain with the phosphor-MLKL antibody.
evidence: This is shown by co-immunostaining in Figure 2F and is consistent with the lack of RIPK3 expression in these cells.

claim: Cleaved procaspase-3 is detected in wild-type Leydig cells of 18 and 36 month old mice.
source: Cleaved procaspase-3 and cleaved procaspase-8 was detected in the wild-type Leydig cells of 18, and 36 month old mice, while no such signal was observed in age-matched Ripk3-knockout mice (Figure 3A–D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is shown by immunohistochemistry in Figure 3A–D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Cleaved procaspase-8 is detected in wild-type Leydig cells of 18 and 36 month old mice.
source: Cleaved procaspase-3 and cleaved procaspase-8 was detected in the wild-type Leydig cells of 18, and 36 month old mice, while no such signal was observed in age-matched Ripk3-knockout mice (Figure 3A–D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is shown by immunohistochemistry in Figure 3A–D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: No cleaved procaspase-3 or cleaved procaspase-8 signal is observed in Leydig cells of age-matched Ripk3-knockout mice.
source: Cleaved procaspase-3 and cleaved procaspase-8 was detected in the wild-type Leydig cells of 18, and 36 month old mice, while no such signal was observed in age-matched Ripk3-knockout mice (Figure 3A–D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is shown by immunohistochemistry in Figure 3A–D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Cleaved-caspase-3 is detected by western blotting in aged wild-type testes but not in Ripk3-knockout testes.
source: The cleaved-caspase-3 was also detected by western blotting using extracts from the aged wild-type testes but not in Ripk3-knockout testes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown by western blot in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Leydig cells undergo apoptosis as a secondary response to necroptosis in seminiferous tubules during aging process.
source: It is thus likely that Leydig cells undergo apoptosis, as a secondary response to necroptosis in seminiferous tubules during aging process.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Leydig cells show apoptosis markers but do not express RIPK3, and apoptosis is prevented in Ripk3-knockout mice.

claim: Caspase-8 levels decrease in seminiferous tubules showing signs of cell depletion in aged wild-type mice.
source: In aged wild-type mice, caspase-8 levels decreased in the seminiferous tubules showing the sign of cell depletion (Figure 3E and F), and increased in the Leydig cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence in Figure 3E and quantified in Figure 3F.

claim: Caspase-8 levels increase in Leydig cells of aged wild-type mice.
source: In aged wild-type mice, caspase-8 levels decreased in the seminiferous tubules showing the sign of cell depletion (Figure 3E and F), and increased in the Leydig cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The reduction in caspase-8 may explain how necroptosis, but not apoptosis, occurs in the seminiferous tubules of aged mice.
source: This reduction in caspase-8 may explain how it is that necroptosis, but not apoptosis, occurs in the seminiferous tubules of aged mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that caspase-8 levels decrease in seminiferous tubules, which would favor necroptosis over apoptosis.

claim: There is no significant difference between the weights of 15-month-old Mlkl- and Ripk3-knockout mice.
source: There was no significant difference between the weights of Mlkl- and Ripk3-knockout mice, and mice of these knockout genotypes weighed less than wild-type mice at this age (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is measured and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: 15-month-old Mlkl- and Ripk3-knockout mice weigh less than wild-type mice.
source: There was no significant difference between the weights of Mlkl- and Ripk3-knockout mice, and mice of these knockout genotypes weighed less than wild-type mice at this age (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is measured and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The seminal vesicles of 15-month-old Mlkl-knockout mice maintain a youthful appearance, exhibiting the same phenotype as Ripk3-knockout mice.
source: Compared to the obvious aging that had occurred in wild-type mice, the seminal vesicles of Mlkl-knockout mice maintained a youthful appearance, exhibiting the same phenotype as Ripk3-knockout mice (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B with images of seminal vesicles.

claim: Almost all seminal vesicles from 15-month-old Mlkl- and Ripk3-knockout mice weigh less than 1000 milligrams.
source: Furthermore, while the majority of seminal vesicles from 15-month-old wild-type mice weighed more than 1000 milligrams, almost all of the seminal vesicles from age-matched Mlkl- and Ripk3-knockout weighed less than 1000 milligrams (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is measured and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The testosterone levels of both 15-month-old Mlkl- and Ripk3-knockout mice are significantly higher than those of age-matched wild-type mice.
source: Consistently, the testosterone levels of both Mlkl- and Ripk3-knockout mice were also significant higher than those of age-matched wild-type mice (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is measured by ELISA and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Very few (<2%) of the seminiferous tubules from 15-month-old Mlkl-knockout mice are empty.
source: Further, very few (<2%) of the seminiferous tubules from Mlkl-knockout mice were empty at 15 months of age, similar to the tubules of Ripk3-knockout mice, while more than 12% of seminiferous tubules from the age-matched wild-type mice were already empty (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This is observed in histological sections and quantified in Figure 4E and F.

claim: More than 12% of seminiferous tubules from 15-month-old wild-type mice are empty.
source: Further, very few (<2%) of the seminiferous tubules from Mlkl-knockout mice were empty at 15 months of age, similar to the tubules of Ripk3-knockout mice, while more than 12% of seminiferous tubules from the age-matched wild-type mice were already empty (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This is observed in histological sections and quantified in Figure 4E and F.

claim: The fertility rates of both 16-month-old Mlkl- and Ripk3-knockout mice are significantly higher than those of age-matched wild-type mice.
source: Finally, the fertility rates of both 16-month-old Mlkl- and Ripk3-knockout mice were also significant higher than those of age-matched wild-type mice (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is shown in the fertility test results in Figure 4G.

claim: TSZ injection directly into the testis induces MLKL phosphorylation.
source: Injection of TSZ directly into the testis induced MLKL phosphorylation (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is shown by western blot in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Phospho-MLKL is present within the seminiferous tubules of TSZ-injected wild-type testes but not TSZ-treated Ripk3-knockout or Mlkl-knockout testes.
source: Phospho-MLKL was obviously present within the seminiferous tubules of TSZ-injected wild-type testes, but not TSZ-treated Ripk3-knockout or Mlkl-knockout testes, confirming the activation of necroptosis in testes following TSZ injection (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown by immunohistochemistry in Figure 5C.

claim: About 25% of wild-type seminiferous tubules are empty 72 hr after a single TSZ injection.
source: The consequences of necroptosis induction in testes became apparent 72 hr after a single TSZ injection. By this point, about 25% of wild-type seminiferous tubules were empty, whereas almost none of the seminiferous tubules from Ripk3- and Mlkl-knockout mice were affected (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: This is observed in histological sections and quantified in Figure 5D and E.

claim: Almost none of the seminiferous tubules from Ripk3- and Mlkl-knockout mice are affected 72 hr after TSZ injection.
source: The consequences of necroptosis induction in testes became apparent 72 hr after a single TSZ injection. By this point, about 25% of wild-type seminiferous tubules were empty, whereas almost none of the seminiferous tubules from Ripk3- and Mlkl-knockout mice were affected (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: This is observed in histological sections and quantified in Figure 5D and E.

claim: Cells in seminiferous tubules, including spermatogonia, Sertoli cells, and spermatocytes, are stained positive for phospho-MLKL after TSZ treatment.
source: Moreover, when the cells were isolated from a wild-type testis and then treated with TSZ prior to staining with antibodies against phospho-MLKL and cell-type specific markers, cells in the seminiferous tubules, including spermatogonia, Sertoli cells, and spermatocytes, were stained positive for phospho-MLKL, whereas Leydig cells outside seminiferous tubules were negative (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Leydig cells outside seminiferous tubules are negative for phospho-MLKL after TSZ treatment.
source: Moreover, when the cells were isolated from a wild-type testis and then treated with TSZ prior to staining with antibodies against phospho-MLKL and cell-type specific markers, cells in the seminiferous tubules, including spermatogonia, Sertoli cells, and spermatocytes, were stained positive for phospho-MLKL, whereas Leydig cells outside seminiferous tubules were negative (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Three months after TSZ injection, the seminal vesicles of wild-type recipient mice are as enlarged as those from mice older than 15 months.
source: Interestingly, three months after TSZ injection, the seminal vesicles of wild-type recipient mice were as enlarged as those from mice older than 15 months.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A and B with images and weight measurements.

claim: No enlargement of seminal vesicles is observed in Ripk3- and Mlkl-knockout mice three months after TSZ treatment of their testes.
source: However, no such enlargement of seminal vesicles was observed in Ripk3- and Mlkl-knockout mice after the same TSZ treatment of their testes (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A and B with images and weight measurements.

claim: More than 30% of wild-type seminiferous tubules remain empty three months after TSZ injection.
source: Additionally, more than 30% of the wild-type seminiferous tubules remained empty three months after the injection, while those of Ripk3- and Mlkl- knockout mice appeared completely normal without any observable loss of cells (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This is observed in histological sections and quantified in Figure 6C and D.

claim: Seminiferous tubules of Ripk3- and Mlkl-knockout mice appear completely normal without any observable loss of cells three months after TSZ injection.
source: Additionally, more than 30% of the wild-type seminiferous tubules remained empty three months after the injection, while those of Ripk3- and Mlkl- knockout mice appeared completely normal without any observable loss of cells (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This is observed in histological sections and quantified in Figure 6C and D.

claim: The lack of regeneration of cells in the seminiferous tubules indicates that necroptosis induction has taken out their stem cells.
source: The lack of regeneration of cells in the seminiferous tubules indicated that necroptosis induction indeed has taken out their stem cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that empty tubules do not regenerate over three months.

claim: Control injection of saline into the testes of wild-type mice does not affect the fertility rate.
source: Control injection of saline into the testes of wild-type mice did not affect the fertility rate and the mice remained 100% fertile, but TSZ injection reduced the fertility rate by 87.5% (only 1 of 8 was fertile) (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is shown in the fertility test results in Figure 6E.

claim: TSZ injection reduces the fertility rate of wild-type mice by 87.5% (only 1 of 8 was fertile).
source: Control injection of saline into the testes of wild-type mice did not affect the fertility rate and the mice remained 100% fertile, but TSZ injection reduced the fertility rate by 87.5% (only 1 of 8 was fertile) (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is shown in the fertility test results in Figure 6E.

claim: 6 out of 8 Ripk3-knockout mice are still fertile following TSZ injection.
source: In contrast, 6 out of 8 Ripk3-knockout mice and 7 out of 8 Mlkl-knockout mice were still fertile following TSZ injection (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is shown in the fertility test results in Figure 6E.

claim: 7 out of 8 Mlkl-knockout mice are still fertile following TSZ injection.
source: In contrast, 6 out of 8 Ripk3-knockout mice and 7 out of 8 Mlkl-knockout mice were still fertile following TSZ injection (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is shown in the fertility test results in Figure 6E.

claim: RIPA-56 blocks the appearance of TSZ-induced phospho-MLKL in the testes in a dose-dependent manner.
source: RIPA-56 blocked the appearance of TSZ-induced phospho-MLKL in the testes in a dose-dependent manner, and was able to completely block necroptosis at the 300 mg/kg dose (Figure 7A, lane 4).
evidence: This is shown by western blot in Figure 7A.

claim: RIPA-56 is able to completely block necroptosis at the 300 mg/kg dose.
source: RIPA-56 blocked the appearance of TSZ-induced phospho-MLKL in the testes in a dose-dependent manner, and was able to completely block necroptosis at the 300 mg/kg dose (Figure 7A, lane 4).
evidence: This is shown by western blot in Figure 7A.

claim: After two months of RIPA-56 treatment, mice fed with RIPA-56-containing diet weigh less than mice fed with control chow diet.
source: After two months, the mice fed with RIPA-56-containing diet weighed less than mice fed with control chow diet (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is measured and shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The seminal vesicles of RIPA-56-treated mice retain their mass (mostly around 1000 milligrams) after two months of treatment.
source: The seminal vesicles of the RIPA-56-treated mice retained the mass (mostly around 1000 milligrams), while the seminal vesicles from mice on normal chow grew significantly during the same period, with majority of them weighing more than 2000 milligrams (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: This is measured and shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: The seminal vesicles from mice on normal chow grow significantly over two months, with majority weighing more than 2000 milligrams.
source: The seminal vesicles of the RIPA-56-treated mice retained the mass (mostly around 1000 milligrams), while the seminal vesicles from mice on normal chow grew significantly during the same period, with majority of them weighing more than 2000 milligrams (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: This is measured and shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: The testosterone level of RIPA-56-treated mice remains high after two months of treatment.
source: Additionally, the testosterone level of RIPA-56-treated mice remained high, while that of control mice decreased (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is measured by ELISA and shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The testosterone level of control mice decreases over two months.
source: Additionally, the testosterone level of RIPA-56-treated mice remained high, while that of control mice decreased (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is measured by ELISA and shown in Figure 7E.

claim: More than 12% of the seminiferous tubules of control mice are empty after two months.
source: Consistently, more than 12% of the seminiferous tubules of the control mice were empty, whereas hardly any seminiferous vesicles were empty in the RIPA-56-treated mice (Figure 7F and G).
evidence: This is observed in histological sections and quantified in Figure 7F and G.

claim: Hardly any seminiferous vesicles are empty in RIPA-56-treated mice after two months.
source: Consistently, more than 12% of the seminiferous tubules of the control mice were empty, whereas hardly any seminiferous vesicles were empty in the RIPA-56-treated mice (Figure 7F and G).
evidence: This is observed in histological sections and quantified in Figure 7F and G.

claim: 19 out of 25 mice (76%) on the RIPA-56 diet are fertile after two months of treatment.
source: Finally, the fertility rates of the RIPA-56-treated mice were much higher than those of control mice with 19 out of 25 mice (76%) on the RIPA-56 diet were fertile while only 6 out of 23 mice (26%) on normal diet produced progeny (Figure 7H).
evidence: This is shown in the fertility test results in Figure 7H.

claim: Only 6 out of 23 mice (26%) on normal diet produce progeny after two months.
source: Finally, the fertility rates of the RIPA-56-treated mice were much higher than those of control mice with 19 out of 25 mice (76%) on the RIPA-56 diet were fertile while only 6 out of 23 mice (26%) on normal diet produced progeny (Figure 7H).
evidence: This is shown in the fertility test results in Figure 7H.

claim: At 18 months of age, 10 out of 15 mice (67%) on RIPA-56 diet still produce progenies.
source: After 5 months, the difference in fertility was even more dramatic between mice on RIPA-56-containing and the ones on normal chow diet. At age of 18 months, 10 out of 15 mice (67%) on RIPA 56 diet still produced progenies while only 2 out of 15 mice (13%) on normal chow diet did (Figure 7I).
evidence: This is shown in the fertility test results in Figure 7I.

claim: At 18 months of age, only 2 out of 15 mice (13%) on normal chow diet produce progenies.
source: After 5 months, the difference in fertility was even more dramatic between mice on RIPA-56-containing and the ones on normal chow diet. At age of 18 months, 10 out of 15 mice (67%) on RIPA 56 diet still produced progenies while only 2 out of 15 mice (13%) on normal chow diet did (Figure 7I).
evidence: This is shown in the fertility test results in Figure 7I.

claim: Abundant phospho-MLKL signals are observed in testes from 18-month-old mice on normal chow.
source: Consistently, when we stained the testes from these mice with the anti-phospho-MLKL antibody, we observed abundant signals from the testes of mice on normal chow whereas hardly any phospho-MLKL signal was seen in mice on RIPA-56-containing diet (Figure 7J and K).
evidence: This is shown by immunohistochemistry in Figure 7J and quantified in Figure 7K.

claim: Hardly any phospho-MLKL signal is seen in testes from 18-month-old mice on RIPA-56-containing diet.
source: Consistently, when we stained the testes from these mice with the anti-phospho-MLKL antibody, we observed abundant signals from the testes of mice on normal chow whereas hardly any phospho-MLKL signal was seen in mice on RIPA-56-containing diet (Figure 7J and K).
evidence: This is shown by immunohistochemistry in Figure 7J and quantified in Figure 7K.

claim: Necroptosis is a form of programmed necrotic cell death caused by the tumor necrosis factor family of cytokines.
source: Necroptosis is a form of programmed necrotic cell death caused by the tumor necrosis factor family of cytokines (Christofferson and Yuan, 2010; Vandenabeele et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: RIPK1 is recruited to the cytosolic side of TNF receptor family members and its kinase activity is activated in response to receptor activation.
source: In response to the activation of TNF receptor family members, receptor-interacting kinase 1 (RIPK1) is recruited to the cytosolic side of the receptor and its kinase activity is activated (Holler et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citation.

claim: RIPK1 interacts with and phosphorylates RIPK3, leading to its activation.
source: RIPK1 then interacts with and phosphorylates a related kinase, RIPK3, leading to its activation (Cho et al., 2009; Degterev et al., 2008; He et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: If cells have their caspase-8 activity inhibited, RIPK3 drives the cell fate towards necroptosis.
source: If the cells also happen to have their caspase-8 activity inhibited, either through interaction with its cellular inhibitor cFLIP or through the action of viral or chemical inhibitors, RIPK3 drives the cell fate towards necroptosis (He et al., 2009; Holler et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Necroptosis can be inhibited by RIPK1 kinase inhibitor compounds.
source: Necroptosis can be inhibited by RIPK1 kinase inhibitor compounds, and can be promoted by small molecule Smac mimetics, which shifts RIPK1 function from NF-κB activation to activation of RIPK3 (Degterev et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Necroptosis can be promoted by small molecule Smac mimetics, which shift RIPK1 function from NF-κB activation to activation of RIPK3.
source: Necroptosis can be inhibited by RIPK1 kinase inhibitor compounds, and can be promoted by small molecule Smac mimetics, which shifts RIPK1 function from NF-κB activation to activation of RIPK3 (Degterev et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: RIPK3 phosphorylates MLKL on serine 357 and threonine 358 of human MLKL or the mouse equivalent of serine 345, serine 347, and threonine 349.
source: Once active, RIPK3 then phosphorylates a pseudokinase called mixed lineage kinase domain-like protein (MLKL) (Sun et al., 2012). MLKL normally exists as an inactive monomer in the cytosol. Upon RIPK3 phosphorylation on serine 357 and threonine 358 of human MLKL or the mouse equivalent of serine 345, serine 347, and threonine 349, MLKL forms oligomers and translocates to the plasma membrane, where it disrupts membrane integrity, resulting in necrotic cell death (Cai et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2014; Hildebrand et al., 2014; Murphy et al., 2013; Rodriguez et al., 2016; Sun et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Upon RIPK3 phosphorylation, MLKL forms oligomers and translocates to the plasma membrane, where it disrupts membrane integrity, resulting in necrotic cell death.
source: Upon RIPK3 phosphorylation on serine 357 and threonine 358 of human MLKL or the mouse equivalent of serine 345, serine 347, and threonine 349, MLKL forms oligomers and translocates to the plasma membrane, where it disrupts membrane integrity, resulting in necrotic cell death (Cai et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2014; Hildebrand et al., 2014; Murphy et al., 2013; Rodriguez et al., 2016; Sun et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Ripk3 knockout mice show defects in defending microbial infections.
source: Necroptosis is known to have important functions under pathological conditions of microbial infections or tissue damage since Ripk3 knockout mice show defects in defending microbial infections or manifest less tissue damage in a variety of chemical or ischemic reperfusion induced tissue damage models (Cho et al., 2009; He et al., 2009; Robinson et al., 2012; Upton et al., 2010; Zhou and Yuan, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Ripk3 knockout mice manifest less tissue damage in a variety of chemical or ischemic reperfusion induced tissue damage models.
source: Necroptosis is known to have important functions under pathological conditions of microbial infections or tissue damage since Ripk3 knockout mice show defects in defending microbial infections or manifest less tissue damage in a variety of chemical or ischemic reperfusion induced tissue damage models (Cho et al., 2009; He et al., 2009; Robinson et al., 2012; Upton et al., 2010; Zhou and Yuan, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Mice with Ripk3 or Mlkl gene knockout are remarkably normal without any noticeable developmental, physiological, or fertility defects.
source: However, mice with Ripk3 or Mlkl gene knockout are remarkably normal without any noticeable developmental, physiological, or fertility defects (Murphy et al., 2013; Newton et al., 2004; Wu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: An elevated TNF-α level is observed in the old testis of wild-type mice.
source: Indeed, we observed an elevated TNF-α level in the old testis of wild-type mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by western blot in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: No elevation of TNF-α is seen in the testis of age-matched Ripk3-knockout mice.
source: Interestingly, no such elevation was seen in the testis of age-matched Ripk3-knockout mice, indicating that such an elevation may be augmented through a feed forward mechanism.
evidence: This is shown by western blot in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The elevation of TNF-α in old wild-type testis may be augmented through a feed forward mechanism.
source: Interestingly, no such elevation was seen in the testis of age-matched Ripk3-knockout mice, indicating that such an elevation may be augmented through a feed forward mechanism.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that TNF-α elevation is absent in Ripk3-knockout mice.

claim: Necroptosis-instigated reproductive system aging effectively eliminates old animals from the reproductive pool.
source: Necroptosis-instigated reproductive system aging effectively eliminates old animals from the reproductive pool.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overall findings of the study.

claim: Elimination of old animals from the mating pool results in healthier pups overall, conferring an evolutionary advantage.
source: Given that aged animals carry significantly more DNA damage than younger animals, their elimination from the mating pool results in healthier pups overall, an outcome that would confer an evolutionary advantage over (a population) of animals that do not thusly employ a necroptosis program in their testes.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the observation that aged mice produce less healthy offspring.
